35-shots-of-rum-2009.gazette: Denis filmed a working-class Afro-Parisian household in the towers north of Paris, where the commuter line runs close enough to count as furniture. The father drives an RER train; the film gives his shift the same weight it gives dinner. Almost nothing gets explained, because inside the apartment nothing needs to be.

about-elly-2009.gazette: Farhadi put a group of Tehran professionals in a rented villa on the Caspian coast and let the takes run while they talked over each other. The disappearance at the center is never handed down as a verdict; the ensemble simply keeps arguing about what happened and who lied first. No character is written to be the one who is right.

everyone-else-2009.gazette: Ade's couple take a holiday at a family house in Sardinia, and the island is denied its postcard entirely — no vistas, no lighting scheme, just heat and a half-finished room. The performances were built by observation rather than by beats, in the Berlin School habit of letting a scene run well past its point. The pressure comes from proximity, not plot.
everyone-else-2009.prism: The cost of that method lands on the actors: with no story to hide behind, every awkward silence is theirs to carry. The audience ends up watching two people be embarrassing rather than watching a film about embarrassment.

the-time-that-remains-2009.gazette: The house in Nazareth is Suleiman's own, and the script comes out of his father's diaries. The 1948 passages stage the fall of the city as family memory rather than national epic — a surrender signed in a room, a fighter's rifle put away. The record and the set share an address.

carlos-2010.gazette: Assayas followed Ilich Ramírez Sánchez along the documented itinerary: safe houses, borrowed passports, the 1975 raid on OPEC headquarters in Vienna and the plane that carried the hostages out. The full cut runs five and a half hours, roughly because the record does not compress well. Ramírez, serving life in France, objected to the film.

the-king-s-speech-2010.gazette: The film tracks George VI's work with speech therapist Lionel Logue toward the broadcast announcing war in September 1939. Logue's treatment actually began in 1926, a decade earlier than the abdication crisis the film squeezes it into, and Churchill, shown throughout as a sympathetic ally, had in fact backed Edward VIII. Best Picture followed regardless.
the-king-s-speech-2010.prism: Compression is the standard biopic bargain, and the bill usually goes to the supporting cast — Churchill gets a warmer 1936 here than the one he lived. The stammer is true; the room around it has been tidied.

the-social-network-2010.gazette: Sorkin worked the screenplay up from depositions taken in the lawsuits over Facebook's founding, then kept the deposition rooms on screen as the film's frame. Two incompatible accounts are laid out, cross-examined, and left standing side by side. The legal record supplied the structure as well as the lines.

winter-s-bone-2010.gazette: The Missouri Ozarks supplied more than a location: Granik cast locals alongside her leads and shot inside houses belonging to the families living in them. The livestock, the chainsaws, the porch bluegrass all belong to the region rather than to the production. The realism was borrowed, not built.

a-dangerous-method-2011.gazette: Hampton's screenplay draws on the surviving Freud–Jung correspondence and on Sabina Spielrein's own diaries and letters, which sat in a Geneva basement until 1977. A good deal of what the three say to each other on screen exists on paper. The episode the profession spent decades declining to discuss is now the plot.
a-dangerous-method-2011.prism: Spielrein got her documents back long before she got her standing — she practiced as a physician and analyst in her own right, and the same archive that recovered her also fixed her, on screen, as the patient between two men. Preservation and reduction came out of the same box.

a-separation-2011.gazette: A dispute between a Tehran household and its hired caregiver escalates through the civil courts, filmed in cramped rooms at roughly witness distance. Each side arrives with documents, injuries, and a version. Nothing in the script arbitrates, and the final choice is left off screen.

hugo-2011.gazette: Georges Méliès finished his working life selling toys from a kiosk in a Paris railway station, his film stock long since burned or sold off for its celluloid. Scorsese put that decline on screen as fact rather than atmosphere, along with the rediscovery, the gala, the Legion of Honour. A children's adventure was assembled around a film-preservation case file.

meek-s-cutoff-2011.gazette: In 1845 Stephen Meek led a wagon party off the Oregon Trail on a shortcut across the high desert, and the crossing cost lives to thirst, bad water, and delay. Reichardt keeps the pace of that route and gives the party's Cayuse captive dialogue without subtitles. The boxed 1.33 frame narrows the horizon to what a bonnet allows.
meek-s-cutoff-2011.prism: Withholding the subtitles drops the audience exactly where the settlers stood, which is the point and also the ceiling — the one person who may know the way stays unreadable for the length of the film. The film shares their ignorance instead of correcting it.

moneyball-2011.gazette: The 2002 Oakland Athletics lost three stars to free agency and answered with on-base percentage, and the film keeps the real names, the real numbers, and Beane's documented refusal to watch his own team play. Lewis reported the season first; the arithmetic on screen is his. The twenty-game win streak required no dramatization.

play-2011.gazette: Gothenburg police in the late 2000s had a name for the routine: the little-brother trick. No weapons and no blows, just a story about a stolen phone and a walk that kept going, run on other children in the city center between 2006 and 2008. Östlund built the film from those case files and shot the encounters in long static takes, where the robbery turns out to be mostly conversation.

the-intouchables-2011.gazette: Philippe Pozzo di Borgo, a champagne-house executive, was left quadriplegic by a paragliding crash in 1993 and hired Abdel Sellou, recently out of prison, as his live-in carer. Footage of the two real men runs over the closing credits, which is where the fiction hands the record back. Sellou is Algerian; the film made its carer Senegalese.
the-intouchables-2011.prism: That swap is the film's quietest edit — a man from an Algerian family in the Paris banlieue becomes a Senegalese one, and plenty of critics on both sides of the Atlantic read the result as a type rather than a person. The credits footage proves the friendship happened; it can't prove the portrait is fair.
